title: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson Issues Proclamation Recognising Diwali; Cook County Follows
excerpt: The mayor's proclamation, dated November 23, honours Diwali's significance for Hindu and Jain communities and acknowledges the Sikh observance of Bandi Chhor Divas; a companion Cook County resolution was adopted on November 19.
body:
• Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson issued a proclamation dated November 23, 2026 recognising Diwali and urging residents to celebrate the traditions that enrich the city's neighbourhoods.
  • Cook County adopted a companion resolution on November 19, sponsored by Commissioner Tara S. Stamps, honouring the festival and South Asian contributions to civic and economic life.
  • The proclamation notes Diwali's significance for Hindu and Jain communities and separately acknowledges the Sikh observance of Bandi Chhor Divas.
  • The recognition came weeks after an attempted mass shooting at the Sri Venkateswara Temple in Aurora, and days after FBI officials met Hindu community leaders about temple safety.

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson has issued a proclamation recognising Diwali, describing the festival as holding deep spiritual, cultural and religious significance for the city's Hindu and Jain communities and urging residents to celebrate the diverse traditions that enrich Chicago's neighbourhoods. The proclamation is dated Monday, November 23, 2026, according to IANS.

"The City of Chicago embraces the many cultural and faith traditions represented throughout our neighbourhoods and recognises that celebrating our differences promotes mutual understanding, strengthens community connections, and reinforces our shared commitment to an inclusive city where all residents are valued," Johnson said, in remarks reported by BusinessLine.

A county resolution alongside

Cook County, which includes Chicago, adopted a companion resolution on November 19, sponsored by Commissioner Tara S. Stamps of the 1st District, recognising cooperation between her office and the mayor's office in honouring the festival. Both documents praise South Asian communities for their contributions through, in the proclamation's words, "civic leadership, entrepreneurship, public service, the arts, faith institutions, and community engagement." The mayor's proclamation describes Diwali as representing light, hope and new beginnings, with an emphasis on family, unity and compassion. It also notes that Sikh communities commemorate Bandi Chhor Divas in the same festive season, honouring the ideals of freedom and liberation.

Recognition after an attack plot

The proclamation came weeks after a teenager attempted a mass shooting at the Sri Venkateswara Temple in Aurora, in the Chicago metropolitan area. Last week, officials from the FBI's Chicago field office met members of the Hindu community to discuss temple safety and security, hate-crime reporting, and situational awareness for places of worship and festivals. The outreach came on November 20, a day after the teenager, Alexandros Paporakis, was indicted for plotting to attack the temple.

"We're grateful to the Aurora and Naperville Police Departments and the FBI for meeting with us and representatives from 30 local Hindu organisations."

— Suhag Shukla, Executive Director, Hindu American Foundation

For Chicago's South Asian community — one of the largest in the Midwest, anchored by neighbourhoods such as Devon Avenue — the paired city and county documents put the festival on the civic calendar in the same season that temple security has become a live concern. The proclamation is a recognition, not a holiday declaration: it does not create a city holiday or change school or office schedules. Its practical effect is ceremonial and symbolic, placing Diwali alongside the other faith and cultural observances the city formally marks each year.
